Let \(p\): Nagpur is in Maharashtra; \(q\): Chennai is in Tamilnadu. The statement uses "and", so symbolically it is \(p \wedge q\).
Let \(p\): Triangle is equilateral; \(q\): Triangle is isosceles. The statement uses "or", so symbolically it is \(p \vee q\).
Let \(p\): The angle is a right angle; \(q\): It is of measure \(90^\circ\). "if and only if" is the biconditional, so symbolically it is \(p \leftrightarrow q\).
Let \(p\): Angle is acute; \(q\): Angle is obtuse. "neither ... nor" negates both, so symbolically it is \(\sim p \wedge \sim q\).
Let \(p\): \(\Delta ABC\) is right angled at B; \(q\): \(m\angle A + m\angle C = 90^\circ\). "If ... then" is the conditional, so symbolically it is \(p \to q\).
Let \(p\): Hima Das wins gold medal; \(q\): She runs fast. "if and only if" is the biconditional, so symbolically it is \(p \leftrightarrow q\).
Let \(p\): \(x\) is an irrational number; \(q\): \(x\) is a square of an integer. "not ... but" gives \(\sim p \wedge q\).
"4 is odd" is F and "1 is prime" is F (1 is not prime). A disjunction \(\vee\) is true only if at least one part is true; here \(F \vee F = F\). Truth value: F.
"64 is a perfect square" is T (\(8^2 = 64\)) and "46 is a prime number" is F (\(46 = 2 \times 23\)). A conjunction \(\wedge\) needs both true; here \(T \wedge F = F\). Truth value: F.
"5 is a prime number" is T and "7 divides 94" is F (\(94 = 7 \times 13 + 3\)). A conjunction \(\wedge\) needs both true; here \(T \wedge F = F\). Truth value: F.
Let \(p\): \(5 - 3i\) is a real number, which is F (it has a non-zero imaginary part). The statement is \(\sim p\), so its truth value is \(\sim F = T\). Truth value: T.
"\(3 \times 5 = 8\)" is F and "\(3 + 5 = 15\)" is F. A conditional \(p \to q\) with a false antecedent is true; here \(F \to F = T\). Truth value: T.
"Milk is white" is T and "sky is blue" is T. A biconditional \(\leftrightarrow\) is true when both parts have the same truth value; here \(T \leftrightarrow T = T\). Truth value: T.
"24 is a composite number" is T (\(24 = 2^3 \times 3\)) and "17 is a prime number" is T. A disjunction \(\vee\) is true if at least one part is true; here \(T \vee T = T\). Truth value: T.
Given \(p = T, q = T, r = F, s = F\). \(p \vee (q \wedge r) = T \vee (T \wedge F) = T \vee F = T\). Truth value: T.
Given \(p = T, q = T, r = F, s = F\). \((p \to q) \vee (r \to s) = (T \to T) \vee (F \to F) = T \vee T = T\). Truth value: T.
Given \(p = T, q = T, r = F, s = F\). \((q \wedge r) \vee (\sim p \wedge s) = (T \wedge F) \vee (F \wedge F) = F \vee F = F\). Truth value: F.
Given \(p = T, q = T, r = F, s = F\). \((p \to q) \wedge \sim r = (T \to T) \wedge \sim F = T \wedge T = T\). Truth value: T.
Given \(p = T, q = T, r = F, s = F\). \((\sim r \leftrightarrow p) \to \sim q = (\sim F \leftrightarrow T) \to \sim T = (T \leftrightarrow T) \to F = T \to F = F\). Truth value: F.

Given \(p = T, q = T, r = F, s = F\). \([\sim p \wedge (\sim q \wedge r)] \vee [(q \wedge r) \vee (p \wedge r)] = [F \wedge (F \wedge F)] \vee [(T \wedge F) \vee (T \wedge F)] = F \vee (F \vee F) = F\). Truth value: F.

Given \(p = T, q = T, r = F, s = F\). \([(\sim p \wedge q) \wedge \sim r] \vee [(q \to p) \to (\sim s \vee r)] = [(F \wedge T) \wedge T] \vee [(T \to T) \to (T \vee F)] = [F \wedge T] \vee [T \to T] = F \vee T = T\). Truth value: T.

Given \(p = T, q = T, r = F, s = F\). Inside: \((\sim p \wedge r) \vee (s \to \sim q) = (F \wedge F) \vee (F \to F) = F \vee T = T\); its negation is \(\sim T = F\). Also \(p \wedge r = T \wedge F = F\). So the whole is \(F \leftrightarrow F = T\). Truth value: T.
